activities.anchor: nearly all the growth since has been urban
activities.caption: pin the share — the century's denominator
activities.name: urbSharePlace

config.prompt: Around 2008 the urban share of humanity passed the rural one for the first time. By 2050, the UN expects what share of humanity in cities?
config.why: About 68 per cent — and almost every new urban resident is added in Asian and African cities, which is why the coming decades are a question of what those cities will be built like.

activities.anchor: But the deep reason cities keep growing is
activities.caption: pair each concept with its mechanism
activities.name: urbSiteMatch

config.prompt: Why cities exist where they do — pair each concept with its engine:

pairs.right: the ground itself — a river crossing, a sheltered harbour, fresh water
a place's relation to everything else — Singapore's sea lane between India and China
proximity cuts sharing, matching and learning costs at once
second city about half the first, third about a third

config.why: Site explains the founding villages — London at the Thames' first bridging point; situation and agglomeration explain the giants, and the productivity premium is why people pay city rents at all.

activities.caption: rebuild the sequence — the urban cycle
activities.name: urbCycleOrder

config.prompt: The urban cycle, in order from first to last:
items: Urbanisation — rural-to-urban migration and natural growth fill the city
Suburbanisation — cars and railways loosen the pull of the centre
Counter-urbanisation — the leak to small towns and countryside (the 'zoom towns')
Re-urbanisation — deindustrialised docklands rebuilt, the young return
config.why: London's Docklands — abandoned warehouses to Canary Wharf and apartments — is the canonical re-urbanisation; each phase re-prices the land and re-sorts the residents, so 'where people live' is a moving answer.

activities.caption: file each feature under the model that drew it
activities.name: urbModelBuckets

config.prompt: Which model does each feature belong to? File them:

items.label: concentric zones around a Chicago core
a transition zone of looping immigration and decay
sectors bent along tram and rail lines — wedges, not rings
rich and poor corridors running as wedges
multiple nuclei — airports, industrial parks, edge-city malls

config.why: Each model isolates one force — transport cost, succession, corridors, car ownership — and real cities are all of them at once, plus history.

activities.anchor: simultaneously a deprived neighbourhood and an economic engine
activities.caption: call the magnitude — Dharavi's density
activities.name: urbDharaviEstimate

config.prompt: Mumbai's Dharavi packs roughly how many people onto roughly 2 km²?
config.why: Approaching a million people on about 2 km², with informal output estimated near a billion dollars a year — one of over a billion people worldwide living in informal settlements.
config.context: Infrastructure strain and hazard exposure follow the same map: informal settlements often occupy the floodplains, steep slopes and wetlands the formal city rejected.

activities.anchor: The residents are usually the solution
activities.caption: true or false — the clearing debate
activities.name: urbInformalJudge

statements.s: Evicting an informal settlement removes the poverty it holds.
statements.why: Decades of evidence show eviction moves poverty outward without removing it.

statements.s: Dharavi's informal economy runs at an estimated value near a billion dollars a year.
statements.why: A deprived district and an economic engine at once — the two descriptions are not in conflict.

statements.s: Upgrading in place — water, sewers, tenure, participation — can convert a settlement into a neighbourhood.
statements.why: That is the evidence-based alternative to clearing.

activities.anchor: The toolkit is real, and it works better in some places than others
activities.caption: the mayor's desk — pick the lever, own the outcome
activities.name: urbGrowthBranch

config.root: You take office in a fast-growing city of five million. One flagship policy can launch this year.

start.text: What is the crisis you were elected on?

choices.label: Housing costs are exploding
choices.feedback: Supply is the lever — two very different proof cases exist.

choices.label: Traffic is choking the core
choices.feedback: Move people, not cars — there is a Brazilian precedent.

choices.label: Informal settlements are spreading on the slopes
choices.feedback: Clear or upgrade? The evidence has a verdict.

housing.text: Tokyo, with permissive national zoning and constant redevelopment, keeps a metro of 37 million affordable by global standards; San Francisco, with supply restricted, prices out everyone but the well-paid — same demand, opposite rules, opposite outcomes. Singapore goes further: HDB boards house about 80 per cent of residents, the strongest proof that informality is a policy choice, not destiny.

transit.text: Curitiba pioneered bus rapid transit in the 1970s — dedicated lanes, boarding tubes, feeder lines — moving metro-scale passenger volumes at a fraction of metro cost, and structuring the city's growth along the bus corridors. Plan the shape too: Shenzhen was designated a Special Economic Zone in 1980 with roughly 30,000 people; it now holds over 17 million.

informal.text: Eviction moves poverty outward without removing it. Upgrading — water, sewers, electricity, paved lanes, secure tenure, resident participation — converts slums into neighbourhoods; and governance is infrastructure too: Porto Alegre's participatory budgeting (from 1989) let residents steer spending toward the poorest districts.

config.why: Homes, transit, services, tenure, participation — the levers work, but only when pulled decades before the crisis, not after it.

activities.anchor: Sphere of influence can be traced from where shoppers come
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the fieldwork plan
activities.name: urbMeasureSpot

config.prompt: One line of this fieldwork plan is wrong — click it:
lines: Crude density divides population by administrative area.
Built-up density counts population per urbanised km².
Barcelona and Atlanta house similar populations on very similar footprints.
A transect survey outward from the centre usually rediscovers bid-rent in its own data.
Deprivation can be indexed from census indicators such as unemployment and crowding.
config.correction: Barcelona and Atlanta house similar populations on wildly different footprints — which is why their transport systems behave differently.
config.why: A city is a hypothesis about location, and any careful set of measurements will test it — density is the base metric, but which density matters.
